data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"On a clear, calm night the city remains warmer because concrete and asphalt store daytime sensible heat and release it slowly after sunset; the cross-city magnitude of this nocturnal warm anomaly depends mainly on sky view factor, because deep street canyons with low sky view trap longwave radiation and suppress radiative cooling, making the night-time gap larger in denser, taller cities.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If measured nocturnal temperature differences correlate more strongly with anthropogenic heat flux than with sky view factor, this mechanism is insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If rural and urban cooling rates are similar on calm nights despite differing sky view, the storage-release model fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If increases in building height do not produce increases in the nocturnal UHI gap, the sky view explanation is weakened.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"During the day, impervious surfaces with high thermal mass and heat capacity absorb solar radiation. After sunset, the reduced sky view in street canyons restricts longwave radiative loss to the sky, so stored heat is retained longer. This slower nocturnal cooling rate keeps the city air several degrees warmer than open countryside. Cities with lower mean sky view (taller buildings, narrower streets) exhibit a larger night-time UHI because their longwave cooling is more strongly suppressed.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
